                                                  Gwin Cash
                                          Redacted Rebuttal Testimony

    1    Q.    Please state your name and business address.
    2    A.    My name is Gwin Cash. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma City,
    3          Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5    Q.    Are you the same Gwin Cash who filed Direct Testimony in this Case on June 17,
    6          2026?
    7    A.    Yes.
    8
    9    Q.    What is the purpose of your Rebuttal Testimony?
   10    A.    The purpose of my Rebuttal Testimony is to respond to arguments raised by intervenors
   11          regarding OG&E’s proposed XLPL tariff.         I first address the tariff’s application to
   12          incremental load, its minimum billing demand and energy requirements, and the billing
   13          determinants used to develop XLPL class rates.
   14                  I then address the Customer Class Protection Charge, including proposals to reject,
   15          replace, or make the charge symmetrical; the timing and methodology for measuring
   16          customer-class impacts, including the proposed SANCG formula, Customer Impact
   17          Assessment, materiality standard, regulatory accounting, and available annual review
   18          forums; the timing and use of class allocation factors; and the Customer Affordability
   19          Charge and Reservation Charge. I explain why OG&E’s proposed protections should be
   20          retained, why the detailed customer-impact methodology should be developed when
   21          XLPL-scale load is taking service and actual data are available, and how coordinated
   22          general-rate-case and annual review processes can protect other customer classes from
   23          adverse rate impacts.
   24
   25                        INCREMENTAL LOAD AND METERING ELECTION
   26    Q.    What does Mr. Dauphinais recommend regarding the portion of a customer’s load
   27          subject to the tariff?
   28    A.    He recommends that only the post–July 1, 2026 portion of a Type 2 customer’s load be
   29          subject to the XLPL tariff and T&CXLLC, and that the customer be allowed, at its sole

    1          discretion, to delineate that load either by specifying its XLPL load as first through the
    2          meter or by having it separately metered from the remainder.1
    3
    4    Q.    Does OG&E agree that only incremental load should be subject to the tariff?
    5    A.    No. The recommendation is inconsistent with how the protections operate and runs counter
    6          to how any tariff works. The tariff’s protections are not priced against a slice of load. They
    7          are calibrated to the service obligation OG&E undertakes. When an existing customer
    8          qualifies as Customer Type 2, its service is governed by a single ESA with a single Billing
    9          Contract Demand, and OG&E plans and operates that service as one obligation, not as
   10          separate blocks distinguished by when the load arose. The billing minimums, collateral,
   11          and termination fees are sized against the contracted service level because that is what
   12          OG&E has committed to serve. Applying the tariff to the customer’s entire load is also
   13          consistent with OG&E’s standard billing practice: when a customer grows into a tariff
   14          class, its entire load is billed under that tariff, not just its incremental growth.
   15                  Applying the tariff to only part of a customer’s load would leave the remainder
   16          under a tariff that contains none of these protections, while OG&E’s obligation and its
   17          exposure remain undivided.
   18
   19    Q.    What is the difficulty with a customer-elected designation of first-through-the-meter
   20          load?
   21    A.    It allows the customer to determine the extent of its own obligation.                   Under Mr.
   22          Dauphinais’ proposal, the election is at the customer’s sole discretion. A customer would
   23          designate which portion of its consumption counts as XLPL load, and the billing
   24          minimums, minimum demand, and exit fee exposure would attach only to that designated
   25          portion. The customer’s remaining load — served by the same facilities, contributing to
   26          the same peak, and driving the same capacity requirement — would fall outside the tariff
   27          entirely.

    1                  That is not a metering convention. It is a mechanism for reducing the contracted
    2          quantity against which every protection in the tariff is measured, and it operates at the
    3          election of the party those protections are designed to secure.
    4
    5    Q.    Would separate metering resolve the concern?
    6    A.    No. Separate metering changes how consumption is recorded, not what OG&E must build.
    7          Two meters behind one interconnection serving one facility present a single capacity
    8          obligation, and the reserve margin, generation, and transmission OG&E must plan for
    9          reflects the combined requirement.
   10                  The recommendation also sits uneasily with OG&E’s aggregation provision, which
   11          exists to prevent a customer from avoiding the tariff by dividing load across sites. A
   12          customer-elected metering split would achieve within a single site what the aggregation
   13          provision prevents across several.
   14
   15    Q.    Is the July 1, 2026 date relevant in the way Mr. Dauphinais suggests?
   16    A.    No. The July 1, 2026 date identifies when a customer qualifies, not how much of its load
   17          is covered once it does. The Customer Type 2 baseline uses the customer’s maximum
   18          metered demand during the twelve months before July 1, 2026 as an objective reference
   19          for determining whether the tariff threshold is met. That is a qualification test. Mr.
   20          Dauphinais’ recommendation would convert it into a permanent boundary on the tariff’s
   21          application, which is a different function than the date serves.
   22
   23    Q.    PUD witness Scalf’s proposed Customer Impact Review would count only the
   24          incremental load of a Customer Type 2 or Type 3 customer when measuring adverse
   25          impacts on other classes.2 Is that consistent with your position?
   26    A.    It is not inconsistent, because the two positions address different questions. Whether a
   27          customer’s service is governed by the XLPL tariff is a question of applicability and billing.
   28          How the Commission measures whether serving that customer has adversely affected other
   29          classes is a question of methodology. On the first question, the customer’s entire account

    1          is served and billed under the XLPL tariff for the reasons I have explained. On the second,
    2          OG&E does not object in concept to an impact measurement that recognizes that a
    3          Customer Type 2 or Type 3 customer’s pre-existing load was served by existing resources
    4          and paid for under existing tariffs before the customer qualified. But that is a measurement
    5          question, not an applicability question, and the details matter. How incremental load
    6          should be defined, how it applies to a Customer Type 3 customer whose qualifying change
    7          may involve added capacity rather than added metered demand, and how it interacts with
    8          the use of Maximum Contract Demand for cost allocation are all questions that should be
    9          resolved when the measurement methodology is established, as I recommend below.
   10          OG&E is not endorsing Mr. Scalf’s proposed Section 515 or the other provisions of Exhibit
   11          DS-3 by recognizing this distinction.
   12                 That distinction also bears on the concern underlying Mr. Dauphinais’
   13          recommendation. To the extent his concern is that a qualifying existing customer could be
   14          charged, through the Customer Class Protection Charge, for costs attributable to load it was
   15          already taking, the appropriate place to address that concern is the measurement
   16          methodology. It does not require allowing the customer to designate, at its own discretion,
   17          which portion of its load is subject to the tariff’s billing minimums, collateral, and
   18          termination provisions.
   19
   20    Q.    What is your recommendation to the Commission on this issue?
   21    A.    OG&E recommends that the Commission decline to adopt the recommendation. The
   22          XLPL protections are calibrated to the service obligation OG&E undertakes, which is not
   23          divisible by when a customer’s load arose or by how the customer elects to meter it.
   24          Permitting a customer to designate the covered portion at its sole discretion would allow it
   25          to set the quantity against which the billing minimums, collateral, and termination fees are
   26          measured — reducing the protections available to other customer classes while leaving
   27          OG&E’s obligation unchanged.

    1                               BILLING MINIMUMS AND RATE DESIGN
    2    Q.    Why did OG&E propose an 85 percent Minimum Billing Demand?
    3    A.    OG&E must plan and maintain capacity for the customer’s contractual service level. The
    4          85 percent floor ensures a stable contribution toward fixed costs if actual demand falls
    5          below the level for which OG&E planned. It also aligns with the risk-protection structure
    6          of the tariff and is comparable to protections used in other large-load tariffs. As discussed
    7          by OG&E witness DeCourcey in his Direct Testimony, other states have adopted a range
    8          of minimum billing demand requirements; some higher and some lower. OG&E believed
    9          85 percent was the appropriate level given the need for the billing minimums and where
   10          other states have landed.
   11
   12    Q.    The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“PAO”) witness Dismukes recommends
   13          reducing the Minimum Billing Demand to 80 percent.3 How do you respond?
   14    A.    Mr. Dismukes’s own survey supports retaining 85 percent. He finds that approved large
   15          load tariffs impose minimum billing demands ranging from 70 to 90 percent of contract
   16          capacity, and concludes that OG&E’s proposal, while above the median, is still within a
   17          normal range.4 His survey also shows that 85 percent is not an outlier: Ohio Power
   18          Company and Virginia Electric and Power Company have each adopted 85 percent, and
   19          Kentucky Power Company has adopted 90 percent.5 Mr. Dismukes characterizes the 85
   20          percent level as a more conservative application that requires customers to take on more
   21          risk.6 OG&E agrees that it is conservative, and believes that is appropriate for a tariff
   22          whose purpose under HB 2992 is to protect other customer classes from the risk that
   23          projected large loads do not fully materialize — the same risk Mr. Dismukes identifies as
   24          the reason minimum billing demands exist.7

    1                                     MINIMUM BILLING ENERGY
    2    Q.    Please summarize the positions you address in this section.
    3    A.    Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”) witness Dauphinais recommends
    4          eliminating the Minimum Billing Energy provision entirely, characterizing it as
    5          unsupported by analysis, not cost-causal, and rare in practice.8 Google witness Kimbrough
    6          likewise recommends rejecting the energy floor and billing energy strictly on actual
    7          metered consumption and dynamic market prices.9
    8
    9    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais states the provision applies to all base rate and rider energy charges,
   10          many of which recover costs not incrementally affected by serving XLPL customers.
   11          Is that accurate?
   12    A.    No. Mr. Dauphinais’ claim is broader than what the tariff actually provides. The minimum
   13          billing energy provision is designed specifically to not apply to incremental energy costs.
   14          Section 4.02(b) of the ESA states that the Minimum Billing Energy Charge shall only apply
   15          to fixed cost recovery collection in energy charges. Section 4.02(c) then distinguishes
   16          riders that serve as base rate revenue recovery mechanisms between general rate case
   17          filings — the Generation Capacity Rider, Interim Rate Rider, and capacity and purchased
   18          power costs in the FCA — from all other applicable riders, which are calculated using the
   19          customer’s actual measured energy and demand. Charges that recover variable,
   20          consumption-driven costs are billed on consumption.
   21
   22    Q.    Does the Minimum Billing Energy apply to SPP Day-Ahead energy charges?
   23    A.    No. OG&E confirmed in discovery that the SPP hourly Day-Ahead Locational Marginal
   24          Price applies only to the customer’s actual energy consumption adjusted for line losses,
   25          and not to minimum billing energy. Only the PPA and CPA portion of the two-part price is
   26          subject to billing minimums.
   27                 Mr. Dauphinais recommends that, if the provision is retained, OG&E state this
   28          expressly in the Application of Fuel Cost Adjustment section of the tariff.10 OG&E does

    1          not object to that clarification. It reflects the Company’s intent and its billing practice, and
    2          making it explicit removes an ambiguity at no cost to any party.
    3
    4    Q.    Do you agree that an energy floor is not cost-causal because fixed costs belong in
    5          demand charges?
    6    A.    No. The argument assumes a cleaner separation than OG&E’s rate structure reflects. Fixed
    7          costs are recovered through both demand and energy components, and the Minimum
    8          Billing Energy is directed specifically at the fixed cost recovery embedded in energy
    9          charges. Eliminating the floor would not remove that obligation. It would leave a portion
   10          of it unrecovered when a customer’s consumption falls below the level OG&E planned and
   11          procured to serve.
   12                  The rationale is stated plainly in the tariff design: the billing minimums protect all
   13          other customers from stranded costs in the event an XLPL customer’s load is less than what
   14          that customer requested OG&E to plan for, and they ensure OG&E recovers the fixed costs
   15          it incurs to serve the customer even if actual demand or energy falls below the contracted
   16          level. That is a cost-causation rationale, not a departure from one — the costs were caused
   17          by the customer’s own request that OG&E plan and procure for its load.
   18
   19    Q.    Why did OG&E propose Minimum Billing Energy based on a 90 percent load factor,
   20          and do you believe that requirement is appropriate?
   21    A.    Yes. The proposed class is expected to include continuously operating facilities with high
   22          and stable usage, and OG&E must plan substantial capacity and energy-related fixed-cost
   23          recovery around that operating profile. Because fixed costs are recovered through both
   24          demand and energy components, a minimum billing energy obligation is appropriate to
   25          support recovery of the fixed costs embedded in energy-based base-rate and rider
   26          components when a customer’s actual use falls materially below the service level OG&E
   27          planned to serve.
   28                  The 90 percent value is not applied to the SPP Day-Ahead market energy charge,
   29          which is based on actual hourly metered usage. The minimum applies only to fixed-cost
   30          recovery components embedded in energy billing. If the Commission believes additional
   31          clarity is needed, OG&E does not object to tariff language expressly confirming that the

    4    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais notes the 90 percent load factor is high relative to the one comparable
    5          provision he identifies, set at 65 percent.11        Does that comparison hold for the
    6          customers this tariff will serve?
    7    A.    It is a fair observation about the tariff landscape, but it sits uneasily with this record. Mr.
    8          Kimbrough describes XLPL customers as operating at 85 to 90-plus percent load factors
    9          and contributing massive blocks of baseload demand.12 Mr. Dauphinais himself explains
   10          that super-scalar data centers tend to operate at high and steady demand at an extremely
   11          high load factor, in contrast to industrial facilities whose demand is cyclical and tied to
   12          production schedules.13
   13                  For customers with those characteristics, a 90 percent minimum is close to expected
   14          operation and would rarely bind. Mr. Dauphinais suggests that other large loads, such as
   15          crypto-mining operations or traditional industrial facilities, may operate at lower load
   16          factors. But, the Minimum Billing Energy is not keyed to a customer’s industry. It is keyed
   17          to the service level the customer asks OG&E to plan for. Whatever the business, when a
   18          customer contracts for XLPL-scale service, a portion of the fixed costs of serving it is
   19          recovered through energy charges, and a customer that consumes less than the level OG&E
   20          planned around leaves those costs behind for other customers. That risk does not diminish
   21          because a customer’s load factor is lower; it increases, because a lower-load-factor
   22          customer is more likely to consume below the planned level. Exempting such customers
   23          from the floor would reduce protection precisely where the exposure to other customers is
   24          greatest.

    1    Q.    PAO witness Dismukes observes that a minimum billing energy requirement is less
    2          common than a minimum billing demand requirement.                    Does he recommend
    3          eliminating it?
    4    A.    No. Mr. Dismukes notes that only one of the thirteen tariffs he surveyed includes a
    5          comparable requirement and that the PSO settlement tariff does not include one, 14 but he
    6          does not recommend that the Commission reject it; his recommendations are directed to
    7          other provisions.15 He also records OG&E’s discovery response that the 90 percent level
    8          was based on ongoing discussions with prospective XLPL customers, all of which are
    9          expected to have load factors above 90 percent.16 For customers operating as expected, the
   10          floor would rarely bind. It serves its protective function in the circumstance it is designed
   11          to address: a customer whose usage falls materially below the level OG&E planned to
   12          serve.
   13
   14    Q.    What is your recommendation to the Commission on this issue?
   15    A.    OG&E recommends that the Commission retain the Minimum Billing Energy provision.
   16          It applies to fixed cost recovery in energy charges rather than to volumetric costs generally,
   17          it does not apply to SPP Day-Ahead energy charges, and it serves the stranded-cost
   18          protection function that every party in this proceeding agrees the tariff should provide.
   19          OG&E further recommends that the tariff state expressly that the Minimum Billing Energy
   20          does not apply to SPP Day-Ahead Market Price charges, consistent with Mr. Dauphinais’
   21          alternative recommendation.
   22
   23                       CLASS RATE DESIGN AND BILLING DETERMINANTS
   24    Q.    Please explain the intervenor recommendations you address in this section.
   25    A.    Attorney General witness Beling observes that OG&E proposes to establish tariff charges
   26          using minimum billing values while billing customers at the greater of actual usage or those
   27          minimums, and concludes that because actual usage will in many cases exceed the
   28          minimums, the difference produces a planned over-recovery that increases the Company’s

    1          gross profit without offsetting costs allocated to any other customer or class.              He
    2          recommends that the Commission require OG&E to use the greater of actual loads or
    3          billing minimums when developing pricing and charges.17
    4                  Mr. Beling does not seek elimination of the billing minimums.                        His
    5          recommendation is directed at the determinants used in rate design.
    6
    7    Q.    Does OG&E agree that the difference Mr. Beling describes is an over-recovery?
    8    A.    No, and this is the point on which OG&E most respectfully but most firmly disagrees.
    9          Setting rates on the minimum billing determinants is not a device for collecting more than
   10          the XLPL class’s allocated cost of service. It is the mechanism that makes the minimum
   11          bill function as stranded-cost protection at all.
   12                  The arithmetic is straightforward. In any class rate design, the unit rate equals the
   13          allocated revenue requirement divided by the billing determinants. If OG&E divides the
   14          XLPL class revenue requirement by the minimum billing quantities, the resulting rates are
   15          set so that a customer billed at the floor pays the class’s allocated cost of service. If instead
   16          OG&E divides that same revenue requirement by a larger set of determinants reflecting
   17          actual usage, the unit rates necessarily come down — and a customer subsequently billed
   18          at the floor pays those lower rates applied to the minimum quantities. The product is less
   19          than the allocated cost of service.
   20                  That shortfall is precisely the circumstance the minimum bill exists to prevent. Mr.
   21          Beling’s recommendation would retain the floor in form while removing its capacity to do
   22          the work it was designed to do. The customer would still be billed at the minimum — but
   23          the minimum would no longer recover the costs OG&E incurred to serve that customer.
   24
   25    Q.    What is the magnitude of the risk if rates are developed on actual determinants?
   26    A.    It is not a marginal exposure. XLPL customers will be served by generation, capacity, and
   27          purchased power arrangements procured specifically because those customers asked
   28          OG&E to plan for their load, and the fixed obligations associated with those resources do
   29          not vary with how much energy the customer actually takes in a given month. OG&E

    1          incurs them whether the customer runs at a 95 percent load factor or an 80 percent load
    2          factor.
    3                    The structural problem is that the risk runs in only one direction. A customer’s
    4          actual usage can fall below its contracted level for any number of reasons — a slower ramp,
    5          a change in business plan, a shift in computing demand, or a decision to operate fewer
    6          facilities than planned — and under Mr. Beling’s approach OG&E would have set rates on
    7          the assumption that the higher usage would materialize. When it does not, the deficiency
    8          does not disappear. It is either absorbed by OG&E or, in a subsequent rate proceeding,
    9          falls to the remaining customer classes. That is the cost shift HB 2992 directs the
   10          Commission to prevent, and at the scale of a single 1,000 MW customer the amounts
   11          involved are substantial.
   12
   13    Q.    Has Mr. Beling recognized this principle elsewhere in his testimony?
   14    A.    He has, which is why OG&E believes the disagreement is narrower than it appears. In
   15          discussing cost allocation, Mr. Beling agrees that where an XLPL customer contracts for a
   16          certain level and later reduces its actual load, using the Maximum Contract Demand
   17          maintains alignment between the costs assigned to the XLPL class and the generation the
   18          Company would have had to procure, and that this helps prevent cost shifts to other classes
   19          when an XLPL customer reduces its load while still under contract.18
   20                    OG&E agrees with that reasoning entirely. The minimum billing determinants
   21          perform the identical protective function on the rate design side of the calculation.
   22          Accepting the principle for allocation while declining to apply it to rate design would leave
   23          the tariff protected against a load reduction at one stage of the analysis and exposed to it at
   24          the next. Section 509 of the T&CXLLC is designed as an integrated structure — minimum
   25          billing determinants for price determination, Maximum Contract Demand for cost
   26          allocation — and the two halves work together.

    1          proceeding. If actual XLPL class revenues were meaningfully exceeding allocated costs,
    2          that would be visible in those proceedings and the Commission would have the tools to
    3          respond, including adjusting the class’s rates in the ordinary course.
    4                  The Commission is therefore not choosing between Mr. Beling’s recommendation
    5          and an unchecked over-recovery. It is deciding whether to preserve a protection that
    6          operates when a customer underperforms, with a recurring review process available to
    7          address the converse if it arises.
    8
    9    Q.    Is there any accommodation OG&E can offer?
   10    A.    OG&E is prepared to address Mr. Beling’s concern transparently in the proceeding where
   11          it can actually be measured. When XLPL class rates are first developed from a cost of
   12          service study in a general rate case, OG&E will have actual billing determinants, actual
   13          load factors, and actual cost data for the class. At that point the relationship between
   14          minimum-based rate design and class revenues can be examined on evidence rather than
   15          projection, and the Commission can determine whether any adjustment is warranted.
   16                  What OG&E asks the Commission not to do is direct a change to the rate design
   17          determinants now, before a single XLPL customer has taken service, on the basis of an
   18          assumption about usage patterns that has not been tested. The consequence would be to
   19          weaken the minimum bill protection at the outset, and the customers who would bear that
   20          result are the residential, commercial, and industrial customers HB 2992 was enacted to
   21          protect.
   22
   23    Q.    What is your recommendation to the Commission on this issue?
   24    A.    OG&E recommends that the Commission approve the class rate design set forth in Section
   25          509 of the T&CXLLC as filed, under which the minimum billing determinants are used for
   26          price determination and Maximum Contract Demand is used for cost allocation. That
